title.rendered: The Best Pastéis de Nata in Lisbon (2019 Edition)

excerpt.rendered: We ate forty custard tarts in three days so you don’t have to. Here are the six worth crossing the city for.

content.rendered:
Every bakery in Lisbon sells pastéis de nata. Most are fine. A few are worth crossing the city for, and over three days we ate forty of them to find out which.

 

[caption id="attachment_501" align="aligncenter" width="1600"] Fresh from the oven at 7am.[/caption]

What makes a good one

The pastry should shatter, not bend. The custard should be just set, and the top should be scorched in spots, not evenly brown.

Our six

  1. Manteigaria, Chiado. The benchmark. Watch them come out of the oven every few minutes.
  2. Aloma, Campo de Ourique. Slightly sweeter custard, excellent pastry.
  3. Pastéis de Belém. Yes, the queue. It moves fast, and the inside room is huge.
  4. Padaria do Bairro. A neighbourhood bakery that still makes them by hand.
  5. Nata Lisboa. Reliable, open late.
  6. Confeitaria Nacional. Founded in 1829, worth it for the room alone.

Prices ranged from €1.10 to €1.50 a tart. Eat them warm, with cinnamon if you like, and a bica on the side.

Prices checked in April 2019.

title.rendered: Hut to Hut in the Alps: A First-Timer’s Guide

excerpt.rendered: Booking, packing and pacing for your first multi-day walk between mountain huts.

content.rendered:
Walking from hut to hut is the easiest way to spend a week in the high mountains without carrying a tent.

You sleep in dormitories, eat what the warden cooks, and set off again after breakfast.

Booking

Most huts open from late June to mid September. Book at least two months ahead for weekends in July and August, and always tell the hut if you cancel: they will send someone looking for you if you don’t arrive.

What to pack

  • A sleeping-bag liner (required in most huts)
  • Hut shoes or light sandals
  • Cash: many huts don’t take cards
    • Half board usually costs €60–80 a night
  • Waterproofs, even if the forecast is clear

Start early, finish early. Afternoon storms are the rule in July, not the exception.

We’ve put our favourite four-day loop in a separate guide: four days above Chamonix.

This loop links four huts on the south side of the valley. It needs a head for heights on day two and nothing technical otherwise.

DayRouteDistanceAscent
1Les Houches to Refuge de Bellachat9 km1,150 m
2Bellachat to Lac Blanc14 km900 m
3Lac Blanc to Refuge de la Charlanon8 km350 m
4Charlanon to Chamonix11 km200 m

Day two crosses a section with ladders and fixed chains. If that isn’t for you, drop down to the valley and take the lift up again.

For booking and packing, see our first-timer’s guide.

title.rendered: Vienna to Venice by Sleeper Train

excerpt.rendered: Fall asleep in Austria, wake up to the lagoon.

content.rendered:
The night train leaves Vienna a little after nine in the evening and reaches Venice Santa Lucia at about half past eight the next morning.

We took a two-berth cabin. It came with a washbasin, a small breakfast and a conductor who knocked thirty minutes before arrival.

Which ticket

A seat is cheapest, a couchette (six or four bunks) is the sweet spot, and a private cabin costs about the same as a hotel room. Interrail pass holders still need a reservation.

Watch the Alps go by from the corridor window around six. It is worth setting an alarm.

title.rendered: Interrail on a Budget: 10 Things We Learned

excerpt.rendered: How to make a rail pass go further.

content.rendered:
A month of trains around Europe, spending as little as we could. Here’s what made the difference.

  1. Buy the pass in a sale. They come round twice a year.
  2. Pick a flexi pass with fewer travel days than you think you need.
  3. Avoid high-speed trains in France, Italy and Spain: reservations cost extra.
  4. Regional trains are often free with the pass and only a little slower.
  5. Night trains save a night of accommodation.
  6. Bring a refillable bottle and a picnic.
  7. Stations with left-luggage lockers let you see a city between trains.
  8. Book hostels with kitchens.
  9. Many city museums are free on the first Sunday of the month.
  10. Don’t try to see everything. Two nights per stop is plenty.

excerpt.rendered: Early starts, side streets and the temples most tours skip.

content.rendered:
Kyoto has over a thousand temples, and most visitors see the same five. The trick is timing: be at the famous ones when they open, and spend the middle of the day somewhere quieter.

Go early

Fushimi Inari is open around the clock. At 6am you’ll share the gates with joggers and the odd cat.

Go north

Ohara, an hour by bus, has moss gardens and almost no tour groups on weekdays.

Go by bike

The city is flat and the river paths are quick. Most guesthouses rent bikes for about ¥1,000 a day.

Updated for 2022: some temples now require advance booking for the inner gardens.

yoast_head_json.description: How to see Kyoto's temples without the crowds: timing, quieter districts and getting around by bike.

excerpt.rendered: After four years of restoration, the city’s market hall is back.

content.rendered:
Porto’s Bolhão market reopened in September after four years of restoration. The iron roof is the original, cleaned and repaired; the stalls are new, and many of the old traders are back.

Go on a weekday morning for fish, flowers and the best people-watching in the city. There’s a row of small restaurants on the upper level if you want lunch with a view of the stalls.

Open Monday to Saturday, 8am to 8pm.

Two years ago the editorial team agreed to stop taking flights under 1,000 km for our stories. This is what changed.

Trips got longer, and they got better. On the train you arrive in the middle of a city instead of at its edge, and the journey becomes part of the story rather than a gap in it.

It is not always possible, and we still fly when there is no reasonable alternative. But “reasonable” turned out to cover a lot more than we expected.

Editor's note: our Interrail budget guide is a good place to start.

excerpt.rendered: Where to shop, where to eat, and when to go.

content.rendered:
Lisbon has three kinds of market: the old municipal halls where people still do their weekly shop, the food halls built for visitors, and the weekend flea markets.

Municipal markets

Mercado de Campo de Ourique is the friendliest. Shop in the morning; the food counters stay open into the evening.

Mercado de Arroios is the least touristy, with the best fish.

Food halls

The Time Out Market at Cais do Sodré is busy, loud and good for a group that can’t agree on what to eat.

Flea markets

The Feira da Ladra runs on Tuesdays and Saturdays behind São Vicente. Bring cash and patience.
